A1.explanation: `A cos θ` gives the x-component **only when θ is measured from the x-axis**. Here θ is measured from the +y-axis, so the roles swap: the x-component is the one across the angle, `40 sin θ`, and the y-component is `40 cos θ`. Redraw the triangle before writing anything down — this single decision is what makes the incline problems of Chapter 5 come out right or wrong.

diagnostics.a: The y-component is the one along the axis the angle is measured from, so it takes the cosine; a tangent cannot appear in a component at all.
diagnostics.c: A component is a projection, so it uses sine or cosine. A tangent exceeds 1 above 45°, which would make a component larger than the vector itself.
diagnostics.d: You applied the formula for an angle measured from the x-axis. With θ taken from the y-axis, sine and cosine swap places.

A2.explanation: The resultant of two vectors can be anything from `|8 − 6| = 2.0 N` (antiparallel) up to `8 + 6 = 14.0 N` (parallel), and every value in between corresponds to some angle. 15.0 N lies outside that range, so no angle produces it. Magnitudes do not add unless the vectors are parallel.

diagnostics.a: 2.0 N is the minimum, reached when the forces are antiparallel and partly cancel. It is possible, not impossible.
diagnostics.b: 14.0 N is the maximum, reached when the two forces point the same way. Possible, and the largest possible.
diagnostics.d: 10.0 N is the value at 90°, where `√(6² + 8²) = 10`. It is squarely inside the range.

A3.explanation: `F · d = Fd cos φ`, and `cos φ` is negative only for φ between 90° and 180°. At 150°, `cos 150° = −0.866`, so the dot product is negative: the force has a component *opposing* the displacement. This is exactly how friction does negative work in Chapter 6.

diagnostics.b: At 90° the cosine is zero, so the dot product is zero rather than negative — the force has no component along the displacement.
diagnostics.c: At 45° the cosine is +0.707, so the product is positive: the force partly helps the motion along.
diagnostics.d: At 30° the cosine is +0.866, giving a large positive value — nearly the maximum of Fd.

A4.explanation: The calculator's arctan only ever returns an angle between −90° and +90°, because tan θ repeats every 180°. Here `Aₓ < 0` and `Aᵧ > 0`, which puts the vector up and to the left — the second quadrant. Add 180° to the calculator's −45° to get **135°**. Sketching the components settles it in two seconds.

diagnostics.a: That is the raw calculator output, which points down and to the right. Your components point up and to the left.
diagnostics.c: 225° points down and to the left, so both components would be negative. Only `Aₓ` is.
diagnostics.d: 315° points down and to the right — the quadrant the calculator assumed. It matches neither of your component signs.

A5.explanation: A centimetre is 10⁻² m, so a **square** centimetre is `(10⁻² m)² = 10⁻⁴ m²`. Then `2000 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.20 m²`. Squaring the conversion factor — including its power of ten — is the step most often skipped, and it appears in every capacitor problem where the plate area is quoted in cm².

diagnostics.a: You divided by 1000 rather than by 10⁴, which is the conversion for volume-like reasoning, not for area.
diagnostics.b: You used 10⁻⁵. One centimetre is 10⁻² m, so a square centimetre is exactly 10⁻⁴ m² — two powers of ten per length conversion, no more and no fewer.
diagnostics.c: You used 10⁻² instead of 10⁻⁴ — the factor was not squared along with the unit.

A6.explanation: `1.2 × 0.0345 = 0.0414 m²` on the calculator, but for multiplication the answer takes the **fewest significant figures** among the inputs. 1.2 carries two and 0.0345 carries three, so the result carries two: **0.041 m²**. Leading zeros are not significant.

diagnostics.a: That is the unrounded product, quoting three figures. The 1.2 m measurement does not support the third.
diagnostics.b: Four figures claims more precision than either measurement has, and the trailing zero asserts a digit nobody measured.
diagnostics.c: One figure throws away precision you do have: 1.2 supports two significant figures, not one.

A7.explanation: `[v t/x] = (L/T)(T)/L = 1` — dimensionless, so it cannot be an acceleration, which must be L/T². Checking the others: `[v²/x] = (L²/T²)/L = L/T²` ✓, `[x/t²] = L/T²` ✓, `[v/t] = L/T²` ✓.

diagnostics.b: `x/t²` is L/T², an acceleration. It is the constant-acceleration formula with the numerical factor stripped out.
diagnostics.c: `v²/x` gives (L²/T²)/L = L/T², which is exactly an acceleration — it is the centripetal formula of Chapter 3.
diagnostics.d: `v/t` is (L/T)/T = L/T², the definition of average acceleration.

A8.explanation: `|A × B| = AB sin φ`, and since neither magnitude is zero, the product vanishes only when `sin φ = 0` — that is, φ = 0° or 180°. The vectors are parallel or antiparallel. (It is the **dot** product that vanishes for perpendicular vectors.)

diagnostics.a: Two vectors always define a plane, and the cross product is perpendicular to it. Lying in the xy-plane makes the product point along z, not vanish.
diagnostics.b: Equal magnitudes say nothing about the angle, and the cross product depends only on the angle and the magnitudes.
diagnostics.d: Perpendicular vectors give the *largest* cross product, `AB`, and a zero dot product. You have the two products swapped.

B4.model: From `F = ma`, `[F] = ML/T²`; and k is a force per length, so `[k] = (ML/T²)/L = M/T²`. Then `[m/k] = M/(M/T²) = T²`, whose square root is T — a time, so `T = 2π√(m/k)` is dimensionally possible. The other version gives `[k/m] = 1/T²`, whose square root is 1/T, a frequency rather than a period, so `T = 2π√(k/m)` is impossible. Note the check says nothing about the factor 2π.
marks: Dimensions of k derived as M/T² from force per unit length
√(m/k) shown to have dimension T, so the first version survives
√(k/m) shown to be 1/T, so the second version is rejected
